newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS- Brazil affirms commitment to fiscal targets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Brazil affirms commitment to fiscal targets.

text.p: The Brazilian government on Friday cut its 1997 budget by 3.1 billion reais and affirmed its commitment to achieving ambitious fiscal targets.

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir, outlining strict 1997 ministerial budget guidelines, said the spending cuts would ensure the federal government ended the year with a primary surplus equal to 0.8 percent of gross domestic product.
"I would like to make it clear that we will strive for this commitment no matter the circumstances," Kandir told reporters.
Brazil's 431 billion reais 1997 budget was approved by Congress in January and sanctioned by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso last month.

Malan and Kandir, flanked by high-ranking finance and planning ministry officials, said they had decided to cut 1.0 billion reais in across-the-board maintenance and running costs and a further 500 million reais from planned investment.
A further 1.6 billion reais in savings would be attained because inflation, originally forecast at 10.6 percent for 1997, was expected to be only 6.3 percent.

Kandir said lower-than-expected inflation would also have an impact on projected revenue, which the government revised down to 173.4 billion reais from the 178.8 billion reais contained in the budget approved by Congress.
Total expenditure was changed to 172.5 billion reais from 177.9 billion reais.

Additional revenue from non-tax or social security sources would allow the federal government to generate a primary surplus of 6.677 billion reais, equivalent to 0.8 percent of GDP, the two ministries said in a joint statement.
The ministerial spending guidelines, due to be sent to Cardoso later Friday for his signature, set bimonthly expenditure limits and revenue goals for each ministry.
The program is based on expected 1997 GDP growth of 4.3 percent, up from some 2.9 percent growth last year.
"We have been as responsible as possible in drawing up the spending plans," Kandir said.
The cost-cutting was across the board and not directed at health or education, two areas in which the Cardoso government is often accused of neglecting, officials said.

Payroll costs of 45.1 billion reais, up from 41.5 billion reais in 1996, were not slashed in order to avoid unpleasant surprises, such as a recent Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling granting 11 civil servants a 28.9 percent backdated wage increase.
Still, officials guaranteed that whatever happened, spending on wages and pensions would be limited to 45.1 billion reais, which would allow the 0.8 percent primary surplus target to be met.
"This is the worst case scenario for payroll," said Finance Ministry executive secretary Pedro Parente. "We will not spend more but may eventually spend less."
